title: The extremist risk behind smart glasses
gist: Smart glasses (led by Meta, with Google and Apple entering by 2027) are following the same adoption-to-weaponization pattern as commercial drones — the January 2025 New Orleans attacker wore Meta smart glasses recording footage before the attack — and the author argues the security risk isn't new capability but making existing capabilities (hands-free filming, real-time AI processing) cheaper and easier for extremists to use.

themes.theme: Smart glasses market growth and the extremist adoption pattern

insights.claim: Meta currently leads the smart glasses market, but Google plans to launch Android XR-enabled AI-powered glasses later in 2026 and Apple is reportedly preparing its own product for 2027, while inexpensive camera-enabled glasses are already appearing at mainstream retailers like Kmart and Amazon.
insights.speaker: James Paterson
insights.so_what: A competitive-landscape data point for the smart-glasses hardware race and a timeline (2026-2027) for mass-market AI-glasses proliferation relevant to consumer-tech investors.

insights.claim: Violent extremists rarely invent new technologies; instead they adapt technologies developed for other purposes once those technologies become cheap, accessible and easy to use — a pattern already demonstrated with AI, drones and 3D printing.
insights.speaker: James Paterson
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for security-risk assessment: track a consumer technology's cost/accessibility curve, not its novelty, as the leading indicator of extremist-adoption risk.
insights.quote: violent extremists have rarely needed to invent new technologies. More often, they adapt technologies developed for entirely different purposes once they become cheap, accessible and easy enough to use.

insights.claim: Commercial drones followed this exact pattern: uncrewed aerial systems existed as military technology for decades but their accessibility changed dramatically once cheap consumer drones appeared, and extremist groups on the battlefield subsequently adapted them for surveillance, propaganda and attacks, with domestic extremist interest also growing as systems became more capable and easy to obtain.
insights.speaker: James Paterson
insights.so_what: The direct historical precedent the author uses to forecast the smart-glasses trajectory — investors/policymakers in consumer drone and now smart-glasses markets should anticipate similar security scrutiny and potential regulation.
insights.quote: Extremists did not need to develop the underlying technology. Commercial markets did much of that work for them.

themes.theme: Smart glasses as a force multiplier, not a new capability

insights.claim: Smart glasses' security significance is not that they give extremists entirely new capabilities, but that they make existing capabilities — hands-free photography, video recording, communication — easier, less conspicuous and increasingly integrated with AI.
insights.speaker: James Paterson
insights.so_what: Frames smart glasses as an incremental rather than categorical security risk — useful for calibrating proportionate policy response versus overreaction.
insights.quote: Their significance is not that they give extremists entirely new capabilities, but that they make existing ones easier to use.

insights.claim: Months before the January 2025 New Orleans attack, Shamsud-Din Jabbar travelled through the French Quarter wearing Meta smart glasses recording footage as he cycled through the area, providing an early real-world example of consumer AI wearables being incorporated into attack planning (though the glasses were not essential to the attack itself).
insights.speaker: James Paterson
insights.so_what: A concrete, named case establishing smart-glasses use in real terrorist attack planning — a citable precedent for security agencies and smart-glasses manufacturers assessing misuse risk and possible content/data retention policies.
insights.locator: paragraph on the New Orleans attack example

insights.claim: The potential integration of AI into smart glasses may expand their extremist utility further by allowing footage and information to be processed in real time rather than simply recorded, reinforcing the propaganda dimension of extremist violence (as seen in the continued circulation of 2019 Christchurch attack footage).
insights.speaker: James Paterson
insights.so_what: Flags real-time AI processing on wearables as the next-stage risk to monitor, beyond simple recording — relevant to AI-safety and content-moderation policy for wearable-AI makers.
insights.locator: paragraph on AI integration and propaganda

insights.claim: The latest UN General Assembly session explicitly raised concerns about terrorist exploitation of emerging technologies and called on states to consider additional measures to address their misuse.
insights.speaker: James Paterson
insights.so_what: Signals incoming international policy attention to emerging consumer tech misuse, which could translate into future regulatory requirements for smart glasses and similar AI wearables.
insights.locator: paragraph on UN General Assembly recognition

insights.claim: Governments have often struggled to identify the security implications of new technologies before widespread adoption, since responses tend to focus on individual technologies or specific harms while extremist-use risk only becomes obvious once a technology is already widely available.
insights.speaker: James Paterson
insights.so_what: A structural critique of reactive tech-security policymaking — implies a first-mover advantage exists for governments/firms that build proactive risk-assessment frameworks (price, availability, ease of use) before mass adoption.
insights.quote: A capability that currently requires specialist knowledge may present a different security problem if commercial development in future makes it usable by almost anyone.
